identity_notes: The retrieved literature for 'garcinia_cambogia' is heavily contaminated (82 of 122 records) by two taxonomically distinct Garcinia species with entirely different active compounds and indications: Garcinia mangostana (mangosteen; xanthones/alpha-mangostin, studied for schizophrenia/bipolar depression, periodontal disease, antimicrobial/anticancer effects) and Garcinia kola (bitter kola; kolaviron, studied for cardiovascular/hepatic/reproductive protection and glaucoma) — both rejected here as different_substance since 'Garcinia cambogia' on a supplement label refers specifically to hydroxycitric-acid-containing G. cambogia, not these other species. The single most important applicability caveat for the genuine G. cambogia/HCA evidence base: a recurring and serious hepatotoxicity signal exists across multiple independent case series (four cases of acute liver failure in PMID 29802521, one requiring transplant in the related fat-burner case series PMID 29310849, plus PMID 31879192 and a regulatory-alert review PMID 35710615 tracing European food-safety alerts from 2009 onward), despite most randomized efficacy trials themselves reporting no significant adverse events at typical doses (up to 2800 mg/day). Efficacy findings for weight/fat loss are consistently small in magnitude and inconsistent across trials (the largest single RCT, n=135, found NO significant weight-loss benefit over placebo), and many 'positive' trials tested Garcinia cambogia only as one component of multi-ingredient combination products (with glucomannan, orlistat, silodosin, chromium, Gymnema sylvestre, green tea, green coffee, L-carnitine, etc.) rather than as an isolated ingredient.
